Front: Five tiers of lawyer discipline, lightest to heaviest
Back: Probation → private reprimand (act published, not the lawyer's name) → public reprimand → suspension → disbarment.

Front: Is disbarment permanent? How does a lawyer get reinstated?
Back: No. After 5 years the lawyer may apply. Must prove by clear and convincing evidence (1) rehabilitation AND (2) compliance with all conditions.

Front: Does discipline require harm to a client? Does malpractice?
Back: Discipline: no harm required. Malpractice: harm and causation required.

Front: UPL: what's the general rule and the one universal exception?
Back: Most states bar nonlawyers from practicing law (no settled definition of “practice of law”). Exception: you may always represent yourself.

Front: UPL: are legal advice books and legal software allowed?
Back: Books: allowed in most jurisdictions. Software: generally OK; some states have tried to ban it, and how far it may go is an open question.

Front: Rule 5.5 cmt. [2]: purpose of UPL rules
Back: Limiting practice to bar members protects the public against legal services by unqualified persons. → UPL rules protect the public, not lawyers' business.

Nonlawyers MAY sell legal forms and printed material explaining procedure and run a typing service, but may NOT give individualized legal advice. D typed customers' documents, never held herself out as a lawyer. Class point: nobody was harmed; complaint came from lawyers losing business.
Lawyers may work with nonlawyer employees if lawyers run the legal services and don't share fees. Lawyer must make reasonable efforts to ensure the nonlawyer's conduct is compatible with the Rules.
(a) No sharing legal fees with a nonlawyer. (b) No partnership with a nonlawyer if any activity is the practice of law. (d) No practicing in a for-profit organization a nonlawyer owns an interest in.

Front: Which jurisdictions allow lawyer–nonlawyer fee splitting?
Back: DC, Utah, and Arizona. Everywhere else Rule 5.4 controls.
The Rules still apply when a lawyer provides law-related (nonlegal) services.

Front: How does an out-of-state lawyer avoid UPL in litigation?
Back: Motion to appear pro hac vice (temporary admission). Amended rules also allow temporary practice in some circumstances and full-time practice for in-house counsel.

Front: Birbrower, Montalbano, Condon & Frank v. Superior Court
Back: Representing a client in preparation for arbitration is the practice of law; physical presence is a factor but not required, sufficient contact with the state is enough. NY lawyers advised ESQ in CA under a CA-law contract → UPL, fee agreement unenforceable for the CA work. Legislature later exempted arbitration.

Front: Character & fitness: who bears the burden, and who has the final word?
Back: The applicant bears the burden of proving fitness. Each state's supreme court has the final word. Passing the bar is not enough, and disclosing bad acts is necessary but not sufficient.
Applicant must prove good moral character; past bad acts count even when disclosed. He disclosed settling a case over his father's upholstery business's bad practices → admission denied.

Past serious crime + lack of candor and responsibility supports denial. Killed college students in a marijuana deal, served his sentence; denied for not being forthright about the murders, unpaid child support with excuses, plagiarized brief.

Front: How is a lawyer–client relationship usually formed, and what is NOT required?
Back: Usually through a retainer, but it can form inadvertently (usually to the lawyer's detriment). No written agreement or fee required.

(1) Person manifests intent that the lawyer provide legal services, and either (a) lawyer consents, or (b) lawyer fails to manifest lack of consent and knows or should know the person reasonably relies; or (2) a tribunal appoints the lawyer.

A lawyer retained by an organization represents the organization acting through its duly authorized constituents. Client = the entity, not officers or employees. (1.13(f): may also represent constituents.)

A relationship exists when the client subjectively believes he is consulting the lawyer for legal advice, regardless of the lawyer's intent. Bryan Cave formally declining and Morris having other counsel did not defeat it.
A relationship can arise without a written agreement or fees. Robbins recruited his friend Day as an indemnitor; Day believed Robbins represented him, never got a bill → all ethical duties applied.

Front: Can a court-appointed lawyer decline? What should they do if they object?
Back: Only for good cause (Rule 6.2). Practical answer: raise the objection with the court and let it decide.

Front: Rule 6.2: three good-cause grounds to avoid an appointment
Back: (a) Representation likely violates the Rules or other law; (b) unreasonable financial burden on the lawyer; (c) client or cause so repugnant it would impair the relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent.

Moral or religious objection alone is not enough to decline an appointment (judicial-bypass abortion cases); present the objection to the court. Not compelling: repugnance of subject matter, identity of a person, belief defendant is guilty, view of the civil case's merits.

A lawyer may not decline a client solely because of gender. Firm took only women in divorces; a law office is a place of public accommodation; free speech yields to the state's interest in ending gender discrimination.
(a) is mandatory: “shall not represent” / “shall withdraw.” (b) is permissive: “may withdraw,” allowed even with a material adverse effect on the client.

Front: Rule 1.16(a): three grounds for mandatory withdrawal
Back: (1) Representation will violate the Rules or other law; (2) lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs representation; (3) client persists in using the lawyer's services for crime or fraud.
Must get the tribunal's permission where required, and must continue if ordered, EVEN IF good cause exists. Overrides even a mandatory reason to withdraw.
On termination, take steps reasonably practicable to protect the client's interests.

Front: Is a client's nonpayment alone an “unreasonable financial burden”?
Back: No.
No bringing or defending a proceeding without a non-frivolous basis in law and fact. A good-faith argument to extend, modify, or reverse existing law is fine.

Withdrawal on the eve of trial requires the court's consent and good cause. Whiting (third lawyer) insisted on unsupported claims and planned to sue for malpractice if he lost; withdrawal allowed only because Lacara was stuck between a malpractice suit and frivolous arguments.
Even with good cause, a court may deny withdrawal when trial is close. Lawyer learned weeks before trial the client was lying (possible insurance fraud) → not enough to withdraw.

Front: Class problem 2-10: court orders the lawyer to stay. Answer?
Back: C. He must stay (Rule 1.16(c)).

Front: Class problem 2-11: material disagreement with the client. Answer?
Back: D. Permissive withdrawal is allowed even with a material adverse effect on the client.
(1) Discipline under the Rules: no harm required. (2) Malpractice liability: harm and causation required. Both measure against a reasonable lawyer.
Competent representation requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.

Front: Rule 5.1(c): when is a lawyer responsible for another lawyer's violation?
Back: (1) Orders it, or ratifies it with knowledge of the conduct; or (2) is a partner/manager or direct supervisor who knows in time to avoid or mitigate the consequences but fails to take reasonable remedial action.
Same two tests as 5.1(c), applied to a nonlawyer's conduct that would violate the Rules if done by a lawyer.
Client = principal, lawyer = agent. Firms are vicariously liable for their lawyers' malpractice (§ 58(1)), but not for discipline.
Duty of care + failure to exercise care (breach) + legal causation + injury.

Competence and diligence normally exercised by lawyers in similar circumstances. Violating an ethics rule does not by itself create a cause of action. Higher standard if the lawyer claims special expertise.
A firm is civilly liable for wrongful acts of any principal or employee acting in the ordinary course of business or with actual or apparent authority. Vicarious liability (except NY and NJ).

Front: Bailey v. Algonquin Gas Transmission Co.
Back: The client is bound by the lawyer's neglect as principal, but may recover through malpractice. Lawyer threw away court mail; client lost by default through no fault of her own.

Front: Togstad v. Vesely, Otto, Miller & Keefe
Back: Advice to a prospective client can create a relationship and malpractice liability even if the lawyer declines. “I don't think you have a case” → she waited past the statute of limitations. Lesson: tell them to see another lawyer.
A lawyer may limit the scope of representation if the limit is reasonable and the client gives informed consent.

(1) Prospective limit only if the client is independently represented. (2) Settling a malpractice claim with an unrepresented client only after written advice to seek independent counsel. Arbitration clauses are allowed.

A lawyer may exclude services normally expected under a clear, signed agreement with informed consent. Divorce lawyer's letter said he would not advise on the settlement because he hadn't reviewed her finances → no breach.
Ineffective assistance (6th Am., criminal only): (1) performance below a reasonably competent lawyer AND (2) prejudice, a reasonable probability the result would differ. Prong 2 is the hard one.
Malpractice has a higher burden: lawyer failed to act properly AND but for that failure the result would have differed (vs. Strickland's “reasonable probability”).

Front: Rule 1.2(a): what's always the client's call?
Back: Objectives, whether to settle, and in criminal cases: the plea, waiving a jury, and whether to testify. Lawyer decides the means, after consultation.
[2] On a fundamental disagreement, the lawyer may withdraw or the client may fire the lawyer. [3] Client may give advance authorization; absent a material change, the lawyer may rely on it.

Front: Client says “don't bring me offers below X.” Must the lawyer relay lower offers?
Back: Not required, but should.

Front: Rest. § 21 cmt. d and § 23 cmt. c
Back: § 21 cmt. d: lawyer need not follow an instruction reasonably believed unlawful or unethical. § 23 cmt. c: lawyer may decide for the client when there's no time to consult.

Appointed appellate counsel need not raise every nonfrivolous issue the client wants; issue selection is professional judgment. Dissent (Brennan, Marshall): 6A makes counsel an assistant, so client should control.

Following a client's explicit, informed instructions is not malpractice (unless they require crime or fraud). Clients chose not to raise an absolute foreclosure defense to protect a bonding relationship.
Accepting a settlement without the client's consent violates Rule 1.2(a). Disbarred.
Counsel may not concede guilt over the defendant's express objection. Distinguish Florida v. Nixon: counsel may concede when D, after consultation, stays silent.
May not counsel or assist conduct the lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent, but MAY discuss the legal consequences of any proposed conduct and help the client determine what the law means.
(b) Committing a criminal act (including aiding a client's crime). (c) Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
Exercise independent professional judgment and give candid advice; may refer to moral, economic, social, and political factors, not just law.

Knowingly counseling and assisting a client's crime → disbarment. Told client about a safehouse network to evade custody loss, helped liquidate assets, invoked privilege about her location. Violated 1.2(d), 8.4(b), 8.4(c).

(a) Maintain a normal relationship as far as reasonably possible. (b) If client has diminished capacity, faces risk of substantial harm, and can't act in own interest, lawyer MAY take protective action (e.g., seek a guardian). Permitted, not required.
A competent defendant may waive appeal of a death sentence if the waiver is knowing and intelligent. Mother's “next friend” petition failed because he was competent and had counsel.
B. Objectives vs. means.

A communication initiated by a lawyer, directed to a specific person the lawyer knows or should know needs legal services in a particular matter, offering to provide those services. Targeted + known need + offer.
In person, live phone, or real-time video/audio, with no time for reflection. Does NOT include chat rooms or texts.

Front: Rule 7.3(b): live solicitation ban and its exceptions
Back: No live solicitation when a significant motive is pecuniary gain, unless the target is (1) a lawyer; (2) family, close personal, or prior business/professional relationship; or (3) a routine business user of that type of service.

(c) Even then, no solicitation if the target said no, or it involves coercion, duress, or harassment. (d) Communications authorized by law or court order are fine. (e) Prepaid/group legal plans may use live contact with people not known to need services.

Front: Ohralik v. Ohio State Bar Ass'n
Back: Banning in-person solicitation for pecuniary gain doesn't violate the 1st Am. Lawyer signed an accident victim in the hospital to a 1/3 contingency, secretly recorded her parents.
State may not punish solicitation by a nonprofit lawyer pursuing political/ideological goals (exacting scrutiny). ACLU lawyer offered free representation to women sterilized as a Medicaid condition.
Paying a third party to solicit warrants severe discipline. Lawyer paid a minister to enter hospital areas, pray with families, and hand out his card.

Front: Advertising: which case allowed it, and what are the main limits?
Back: Bates allowed lawyer advertising. No fee comparisons implying your fees are lower; truthful statements can mislead if a reasonable person would expect the same result (disclaimer can cure); no specialist claims unless true AND the certifier is named.
Misleading if it contains a material misrepresentation of fact or law, OR omits a fact necessary to make the statement as a whole not materially misleading.

Front: Rule 7.2(b): five exceptions to the ban on paying for recommendations
Back: (1) Reasonable costs of permitted ads; (2) charges of a legal service plan or qualified referral service; (3) purchase of a practice (1.17); (4) disclosed, non-exclusive reciprocal referral agreements; (5) nominal gifts of appreciation.

(c) No claiming specialist certification unless certified by an approved/ABA-accredited body AND it is clearly named. (d) Every communication names at least one responsible lawyer or firm with contact info.

Trade names OK if no implied government/public/charitable connection; no name of a lawyer in public office not actively practicing; multi-state firms note jurisdictional limits; imply a partnership only if one exists.
False or misleading lawyer advertising isn't protected commercial speech; no actual harm needed. Ads portrayed inexperienced lawyers as experienced trial lawyers.
Hourly; contingent (most common for plaintiffs); flat (routine services); equity interest.

(1) Time, labor, novelty, difficulty, skill; (2) precludes other work; (3) customary local fee; (4) amount involved and results; (5) time limits; (6) nature and length of relationship; (7) lawyer's experience, reputation, ability; (8) fixed or contingent.
Scope and basis/rate of fee and expenses communicated, preferably in writing, before or soon after starting (not needed for a regular client on the same basis). Changes communicated too.
No charging for overhead; in-house services at reasonable cost; third-party disbursements at actual cost; no double billing. Disclose the fee basis at the outset.

Front: 4 hours of work that benefits 3 clients = how many billable hours?
Back: 4, not 12. You can't bill two clients for the same time.
A fee grossly out of proportion to the work is unreasonable. $120,000 on a routine ~30-hour matter, including time learning VT law.
Billing multiple clients for the same time is improper. Billed each of 41 malpractice cases for the entire time he was at court.
Billing for non-legal conversations is improper even if the client was told. $30,000 for weekly life-advice calls while handling a trust → 1-year suspension.

Front: Attorney Grievance Comm'n of Maryland v. Kreamer
Back: Fees must be connected to actual legal work. Billed divorce clients for time filling out her time sheets → disbarred.
Writing signed by the client stating the method: percentages for settlement, trial, appeal; expenses deducted; whether expenses come out before or after the fee. Written closing statement at the end.
(1) Domestic relations matters contingent on divorce or amount of alimony, support, or property settlement; (2) criminal defense.

Front: Three justifications for contingent fees (Rest. § 35 cmt. b)
Back: (1) Access for people who can't otherwise afford a lawyer; (2) incentive to win and screen weak claims; (3) client shares risk with a lawyer better able to bear it.

Front: Can a lawyer raise a contingent fee mid-litigation? What if the client voids the contract?
Back: Late or modified contracts get special scrutiny (Rest. § 18 cmt. e), so no raising fees mid-litigation. Client may avoid the contract anytime; lawyer then gets fair value (§ 39).
(1) In proportion to services OR each lawyer assumes joint responsibility; (2) client agrees, including each share, confirmed in writing; (3) total fee is reasonable.

Front: Rule 1.8(a): business transactions with a client
Back: (1) Fair, reasonable terms fully disclosed in writing; (2) client advised in writing to seek independent counsel, with time to do so; (3) client's informed consent in a signed writing to the terms and lawyer's role.

(d) No media/literary rights deal before the representation ends. (f) Payment from a third party only with client's informed consent, no interference with independent judgment, and confidentiality protected.

Front: Rule 1.8(e): financial assistance to a client
Back: Not allowed, except (1) advancing court costs repayable on outcome; (2) paying costs for an indigent client; (3) modest pro bono gifts for living expenses (not promised in advance, reimbursed, or advertised).

No ownership stake in the cause of action or subject matter, except (1) a lien authorized by law for fees/expenses and (2) a reasonable contingent fee in a civil case. Class examples: interest in a patent or wrestling ring at issue.

Front: May a lawyer take property as a fee?
Back: Yes (Rule 1.5 cmt. [4]), but it may trigger Rule 1.8(a) as a business transaction.

Separate trust account; records 5 years; own funds only for bank charges; advance fees stay in trust until earned; promptly notify, deliver, account; disputed funds stay separate, undisputed portion distributed promptly.

Front: Court-awarded fees: lodestar and who owns them
Back: Courts use the lodestar, with a strong presumption it is sufficient. Fees belong to the client, not the lawyer. A lawyer may agree to waive statutory fees.
Lodestar enhancement only in extraordinary circumstances; a good result isn't enough. Party must identify a factor the lodestar doesn't already account for.

Front: Attorney–client privilege vs. work product vs. confidentiality: what kind of rule is each?
Back: Privilege: rule of evidence (testimony, depositions, document demands). Work product: rule of discovery. Confidentiality: ethical rule.

Front: Work product: what does it protect, and is it absolute?
Back: Materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, including notes and memos reflecting the lawyer's theories and mental impressions. Qualified: a judge may order disclosure on substantial need and undue hardship.

Front: How is confidentiality broader than privilege? How is it narrower?
Back: Broader: covers ALL information relating to the representation, from any source, everywhere. Narrower: some 1.6(b) exceptions are not privilege exceptions.
No. It protects communications, not facts.
No revealing information relating to the representation unless (1) client gives informed consent, (2) disclosure is impliedly authorized, or (3) a 1.6(b) exception applies.

(1) Prevent reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm; (2) prevent client crime/fraud causing substantial financial injury using lawyer's services; (3) prevent, mitigate, rectify that injury; (4) get advice on lawyer's own compliance; (5) lawyer–client claim or defense; (6) comply with law/court order; (7) detect conflicts from firm changes.
Make reasonable efforts to prevent inadvertent or unauthorized disclosure of, or access to, client information.
A communication (1) between client and counsel, (2) intended to be and actually kept confidential, (3) made to obtain or provide legal advice.

Front: Can a client get privilege by hiring a lawyer for any task?
Back: No. Not for work a nonlawyer could do just as well. Ask: is the work primarily legal?
Yes, to nonlawyers helping the lawyer give legal advice: Kovel (former IRS agent at a firm), assistants, accountants, summer associates.
Information meant to go public is not privileged. Discussion of whether to make it public is.
Communication made to (1) a lawyer or someone the client reasonably believes is a lawyer, (2) whom the client consults to obtain legal assistance.

§ 69: communication = any expression between privileged persons (and records of it). § 70: privileged persons = client (incl. prospective), lawyer, and their facilitating agents. § 71: in confidence if the speaker reasonably believes only privileged persons will learn it.
Federal common law governs, except in civil cases where state law supplies the rule of decision; then state privilege law applies.

Privilege covers communications whose predominant purpose is legal advice, even if they touch on policy. County lawyer's emails on strip-search policy → privileged (Fourth Amendment compliance). Special force for government officials.

A corporation can claim privilege over lawyer communications with employees at any level made to secure legal advice. Factors: for legal advice to the company; within employee's duties; employee knew it was confidential; kept confidential. Protects communications, not facts.

When the defense moves or alters physical evidence, privilege doesn't protect its original location. Investigator retrieved a buried wallet; lawyer turned it over but wouldn't say where it was found → must disclose location.

Front: Physical evidence: what does privilege cover?
Back: Communications and observations resulting from them, BUT not where the defense alters or moves the evidence.
